<br>

## Packages

<br>

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

<br>

## Datasets

<br>

The chosen dataset to be studied was **"US Groceries and Gas Prices (2015-2026)."**

We decided that this dataset is relevant to current social and economic issues faced by many U.S. citizens, specifically the increasing cost of groceries and energy.

There are three versions of the same dataset. Three analyses will be performed, and one main dataset will be used to investigate the research question:

**How have grocery and fuel prices changed in the United States between 2015 and 2026, and which categories experienced the highest prices over time?**

<br>

```{r}
avg_item_summary <- read.csv(file.choose(), header = TRUE)
avg_price_monthly <- read.csv(file.choose(), header = TRUE)
avg_price_wide <- read.csv(file.choose(), header = TRUE)
```

<br>

## Average Price Monthly Analysis

<br>

```{r}
avg_price_monthly %>%
  glimpse()

summary(avg_price_monthly)
```

<br>

Some of the columns are not necessary for this project and will be removed, such as *series_id*. Additionally, *year*, *month*, and *category* will be converted to factors so they can be treated as categorical variables during analysis.

<br>

```{r}
avg_price_mo <- avg_price_monthly %>%
  select(-series_id) %>%
  mutate(
    category = factor(
      category,
      levels = c(
        "Meat, broad category",
        "Pork and deli",
        "Beef",
        "Drinks",
        "Dairy and fats",
        "Energy",
        "Fruit",
        "Vegetables",
        "Bakery and grains",
        "Poultry",
        "Eggs",
        "Pantry and snacks"
      )
    ),
    year = factor(year),
    month = factor(month),
    date = as.Date(date)
  )
```

<br>

# Summary

<br>

There are 8,869 observations and 8 variables in the dataset.

The *date*, *year*, and *month* variables describe when an observation was recorded. The data covers the period from 2015 through 2026.

The *item* variable provides detailed descriptions of products, while *category* groups these products into broader classifications.

The *unit* variable indicates the measurement unit associated with the item.

The *price* variable contains the average observed price and serves as the primary variable of interest for this analysis.

<br>

```{r}
dim(avg_price_mo)

summary(avg_price_mo)
```

<br>

## Visualizing Categories

<br>

To understand which product categories tend to have the highest prices, the average price for each category is calculated and visualized below.

<br>

```{r}
avg_price_mo %>%
  group_by(category) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_price = mean(price, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    x = reorder(category, mean_price),
    y = mean_price
  )) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(
    title = "Average Price by Category",
    x = "Category",
    y = "Average Price"
  )
```

<br>

The graph suggests that the **Beef** category tends to have some of the highest average prices among all food categories. To explore this category further, only Beef products will be examined.

<br>

```{r}
only_beef <- avg_price_mo %>%
  filter(category == "Beef") %>%
  mutate(item = factor(item))
```

<br>

## Beef Category Exploration

<br>

The following visualization displays the individual Beef products across time, allowing trends and possible outliers to be observed.

<br>

```{r}
only_beef %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = price)) +
  geom_line(color = "black") +
  geom_point(color = "red", size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~item, scales = "free_y") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Beef Prices Over Time",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Price"
  )
```

<br>

## Distribution of Prices by Category

<br>

A boxplot can be used to compare the distribution of prices across categories and identify variation and potential outliers.

<br>

```{r}
ggplot(
  avg_price_mo,
  aes(
    x = category,
    y = price,
    fill = category
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Price Distribution by Category",
    x = "Category",
    y = "Price"
  )
```

<br>

The boxplot demonstrates that price variability differs substantially across categories. Some categories exhibit wider distributions and more extreme values than others.

<br>

## Price Trends Over Time

<br>

To determine whether prices have generally increased over time, average prices are plotted across the study period for all categories.

<br>

```{r}
avg_price_mo %>%
  group_by(date, category) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_price = mean(price, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = date,
      y = avg_price,
      color = category
    )
  ) +
  geom_line() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Average Price Trends by Category",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Average Price",
    color = "Category"
  )
```

<br>

The trend plot indicates that prices generally increased across many grocery and energy categories between 2015 and 2026. While some categories remained relatively stable, others experienced substantial increases during the observed period.

<br>

# Historical Inflation Analysis

To better understand changes in grocery and fuel prices,
historical U.S. inflation rates will also be examined.

The historical inflation dataset contains monthly inflation
rates beginning in 1914. This allows us to compare the
recent period with earlier economic conditions.

The purpose of this analysis is to investigate how
inflation has changed over time and whether recent
grocery and fuel price increases occurred alongside
higher overall inflation.

<br>

## Loading Historical Inflation Data

<br>

```{r inflation-data}
library(readxl)
library(tidyr)
library(scales)

# Read historical inflation Excel file
inflation <- read_excel(file.choose())

# View dataset
glimpse(inflation)
summary(inflation)
```

<br>

## Cleaning Historical Inflation Data

<br>

The dataset contains monthly inflation observations
and an annual average for each year.

To prepare the data, years after 2025 will be excluded
because 2026 is not yet complete.

The monthly columns will also be converted into long
format to make visualization easier.

<br>

```{r inflation-cleaning}
# Clean annual inflation data
inflation_clean <- inflation %>%
  mutate(
    Year = as.numeric(Year),
    Ave = as.numeric(Ave)
  ) %>%
  filter(Year >= 1914, Year <= 2025)

# Convert monthly data into long format
inflation_long <- inflation_clean %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = Jan:Dec,
    names_to = "Month",
    values_to = "Inflation",
    values_transform = list(
      Inflation = as.character
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Inflation = as.numeric(Inflation),
    Decade = paste0(
      floor(Year / 10) * 10, "s"
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Inflation))

# Check data
glimpse(inflation_long)
summary(inflation_long)
```

<br>

## Historical Inflation by Decade

<br>

To understand how inflation has changed historically,
a boxplot will be used to compare inflation rates
across decades.

The boxplot allows us to identify differences in
variability, median inflation rates, and potential
outliers.

<br>

```{r inflation-boxplot}
ggplot(
  inflation_long,
  aes(
    x = Decade,
    y = Inflation
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot(
    fill = "steelblue",
    color = "black",
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Historical Inflation by Decade",
    subtitle = "U.S. Monthly Inflation Rates (1914-2025)",
    x = "Decade",
    y = "Inflation Rate (%)"
  )
```

<br>

This visualization helps identify which decades
experienced the greatest inflation variability.

Larger boxes indicate a wider spread in inflation
rates, while individual points outside the whiskers
represent potential outliers.

This provides historical context for understanding
recent changes in grocery and fuel prices.

<br>

## Distribution of Historical Inflation Rates

<br>

A histogram will be used to examine how frequently
different inflation rates occurred between 1914
and 2025.

The visualization includes reference lines at
0% and 5% to distinguish deflation from periods
of relatively high inflation.

<br>

```{r inflation-histogram}
ggplot(
  inflation_long,
  aes(x = Inflation)
) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 1,
    fill = "steelblue",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    color = "red",
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 5,
    color = "orange",
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of U.S. Inflation Rates",
    subtitle = "Monthly Observations (1914-2025)",
    x = "Inflation Rate (%)",
    y = "Frequency"
  )
```

<br>

The histogram allows us to examine whether moderate
inflation rates occur more frequently than extreme
inflation rates.

Values below zero indicate periods of deflation,
while values above 5% represent relatively high
inflation.

<br>

## Inflation Frequency Summary

<br>

```{r inflation-frequency}
inflation_long %>%
  summarise(
    Total = n(),
    Below_Zero = sum(Inflation < 0),
    Zero_to_Five = sum(
      Inflation >= 0 & Inflation <= 5
    ),
    Above_Five = sum(Inflation > 5)
  )
```

<br>

## Recent Inflation Trends (2015-2025)

<br>

Since the grocery and fuel price dataset covers
2015 through 2026, a closer examination of inflation
during the overlapping years will be conducted.

This allows us to compare changes in overall inflation
with changes in grocery and energy prices.

<br>

```{r recent-inflation}
recent_inflation <- inflation_clean %>%
  filter(
    Year >= 2015,
    Year <= 2025
  )

ggplot(
  recent_inflation,
  aes(
    x = Year,
    y = Ave
  )
) +
  geom_line(
    color = "steelblue",
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    color = "darkblue",
    size = 3
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = 2015:2025
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_number(suffix = "%")
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "U.S. Inflation Trends (2015-2025)",
    subtitle = "Annual Average Inflation Rate",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Inflation Rate (%)"
  )
```

<br>

The visualization highlights the increase in
inflation during 2021 and 2022, followed by
a decline in subsequent years.

This period is particularly relevant because
the grocery and fuel price dataset also covers
these years.

However, a decline in inflation does not
necessarily indicate that prices decreased.
It may instead indicate that prices continued
increasing at a slower rate.

<br>

## Comparing Grocery and Fuel Prices Over Time

<br>

To compare product prices with inflation, grocery
and fuel prices will be converted into an index
using 2015 as the base year.

An index value of 100 represents the average
price in 2015. Values above 100 indicate that
prices increased relative to the base year.

<br>


```{r price-index, fig.width=12, fig.height=7}
# Calculate average annual price for each item
item_yearly <- avg_price_mo %>%
  mutate(year = as.numeric(as.character(year))) %>%
  filter(
    year >= 2015,
    year <= 2025,
    !is.na(price)
  ) %>%
  group_by(category, item, unit, year) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_price = mean(price),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Calculate 2015 base prices
base_prices <- item_yearly %>%
  filter(year == 2015, avg_price > 0) %>%
  select(
    category,
    item,
    unit,
    base_price = avg_price
  )

# Calculate index for items with 2015 data
price_index <- item_yearly %>%
  inner_join(
    base_prices,
    by = c("category", "item", "unit")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    index = (avg_price / base_price) * 100
  )

# Average indexed prices by category and year
category_index <- price_index %>%
  group_by(year, category) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_index = mean(index, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Plot indexed price changes
ggplot(
  category_index,
  aes(
    x = year,
    y = avg_index,
    color = category
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 100,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "black"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = 2015:2025
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Meat, broad category" = "#D55E00",
      "Pork and deli" = "#A65628",
      "Beef" = "#C2185B",
      "Drinks" = "#7B61A8",
      "Dairy and fats" = "#008837",
      "Energy" = "#009E73",
      "Fruit" = "#E69F00",
      "Vegetables" = "#0072B2",
      "Bakery and grains" = "#56B4E9",
      "Poultry" = "#6A3D9A",
      "Eggs" = "#E7298A",
      "Pantry and snacks" = "#555555"
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.title = element_text(size = 12),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10),
    plot.title = element_text(
      size = 16,
      face = "bold"
    ),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Grocery and Fuel Price Changes",
    subtitle = "Price Index (2015 = 100)",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Price Index",
    color = "Category"
  )
```


<br>

The indexed price comparison helps identify
which grocery and fuel categories experienced
the greatest relative price increases.

Unlike comparing average prices directly,
the index allows products measured in different
units to be compared based on percentage change.

Only products with available 2015 baseline
prices are included in this comparison.

<br>

## Historical Inflation Analysis Conclusion

<br>

The historical inflation analysis provides
additional context for understanding changes
in grocery and fuel prices.

The boxplot and histogram examine inflation
patterns over more than a century, while the
recent inflation graph focuses on the period
relevant to the grocery and fuel dataset.

The indexed price comparison allows us to
identify which categories experienced the
largest relative increases since 2015.

Together, these visualizations help explore
whether grocery and fuel price changes occurred
alongside broader inflationary trends.

However, these descriptive visualizations
do not establish a causal relationship between
energy prices, grocery prices, and inflation.

# Conclusion

<br>

This exploratory analysis examined grocery and fuel prices in the United States from 2015 through 2026.

The results suggest that price levels vary considerably among product categories, with Beef consistently appearing among the highest-priced categories. The boxplot analysis also revealed substantial variation within categories, while the time-series analysis indicated that many categories experienced increasing prices over time.

Future analyses could investigate specific products that experienced the largest price increases and determine whether certain categories were more affected by inflationary pressures than others.
